clue.text: Apocalyptic poet as fairground character

definitions.meaning: George ..., associated with the New Apocalyptics poets of the 1940s
a showman who shouts outside a booth to draw in customers

explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the surname of the poet George Barker; the other is the tout who hollers at a fair to pull in a crowd.

clue.text: De Sade laughingly conceals Forster heroine

indicators.note: the words De Sade laughingly keep the name tucked away inside them, across the word break

explanation.surface: The Marquis de Sade, chuckling, hides a heroine from an E. M. Forster novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conceals' signals letters held inside 'De SADE LAughingly'. Adela Quested is the young Englishwoman in Forster's A Passage to India.
explanation.definitionFit: Adela Quested is the central female character of A Passage to India by E. M. Forster.

clue.text: Forcibly removed from Stevenson

definitions.meaning: a title by Robert Louis Stevenson, the adventure of David Balfour

explanation.definitionFit: The participle means abducted by force, and it is also the title of Robert Louis Stevenson's 1886 adventure novel.

clue.text: Monumental quality of Ben Jonson

parts.note: his tombstone in Westminster Abbey famously reads 'O rare Ben Jonson', so the monument names his quality as being uncommon

explanation.walkthrough: Ben Jonson's gravestone in Westminster Abbey carries the inscription 'O rare Ben Jonson'; 'Monumental' points to that epitaph rather than to grandeur.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun for being rare or uncommon, the quality the Abbey epitaph ascribes to Jonson.

clue.text: Superannuated types like The Old Devils?

definitions.meaning: Kingsley Amis's novel The Old Devils follows a group of elderly Welsh pensioners

explanation.definitionFit: Pensioners who have left work, as are the ageing friends in Kingsley Amis's Booker-winning novel The Old Devils.

clue.text: German version of Shakespeare play

parts.note: a history play by Shakespeare whose title, spelt out in full, reads as if it named a German king

explanation.walkthrough: The history play is usually written with a Roman numeral; spelt out, the title names a king also borne by Germans, so the clue plays on it as if it were a German rendering.
explanation.definitionFit: The full spelt-out title of Shakespeare's history play about the last Yorkist king of England.

clue.text: Stern-sounding character associated with mixed drink

definitions.text: Stern-sounding character associated with mixed drink

parts.words: Stern-sounding character associated with mixed drink
parts.note: Laurence Sterne's hero, whose surname is Shandy, also a beer mixed with lemonade

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stern-sounding' points to the novelist Laurence Sterne; his hero's surname, Shandy, is a British drink of beer mixed with lemonade.
explanation.definitionFit: First name of the hero of Sterne's novel The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy.

clue.text: Fatally impulsive Veronese teenager

parts.note: the young lover from Verona in Shakespeare's tragedy who rashly poisons himself

explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's young lover from Verona, whose haste leads to his own and Juliet's deaths.

clue.text: Associated with departures by 12

parts.note: comings-in paired with exits, as in a title by the poet answering clue 12

explanation.walkthrough: 12 is THOMAS; departures (exits) are the natural partner of comings-in, as in the line 'they have their exits and their ...'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ways in, or arrivals on stage, the natural partner of exits or departures.

clue.text: Keen priced version of opera composer

indicators.note: a new version of the words Keen priced rearranges their letters

explanation.surface: A keenly priced recording of an opera composer's work is on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'version of' rearranges the ten letters of KEEN PRICED. Krzysztof Penderecki was a Polish composer whose operas include The Devils of Loudun.
explanation.definitionFit: Krzysztof Penderecki, Polish composer of operas such as The Devils of Loudun and Ubu Rex.

clue.text: Old flame still attracts Dream character

definitions.meaning: a winged insect that is drawn to a candle
one of Titania's fairies in A Midsummer Night's Dream

explanation.definitionFit: The night insect drawn to a candle, and also a fairy attending Titania in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream.

clue.text: Fatal flaw in Greek drama

parts.note: Aristotle's term for the error or weakness that brings down a tragic hero

explanation.definitionFit: Aristotle's word in the Poetics for the tragic hero's error of judgement leading to downfall.

clue.text: Visionary poet, although not The Rhymer

definitions.text: Visionary poet, although not The Rhymer

parts.words: Visionary poet, although not The Rhymer
parts.note: Traherne, the mystical seventeenth-century poet, shares a first name with the Scottish seer known as The Rhymer

explanation.walkthrough: Thomas the Rhymer was a legendary Scottish prophet; the clue wants another visionary poet with the same name, such as Thomas Traherne.
explanation.definitionFit: Forename of Thomas Traherne, the mystical metaphysical poet, and of the Scottish seer called The Rhymer.

clue.text: Liza of Lambeth

parts.note: the title of Somerset Maugham's first novel, whose heroine's surname is asked for

explanation.walkthrough: Lambeth is a working-class district of south London; Maugham's heroine is Liza Kemp.
explanation.definitionFit: Surname of the heroine of Somerset Maugham's 1897 novel set among London's poor.

clue.text: Retrograde Aym work?

definitions.meaning: a story collection by the French writer Marcel Aymé, the accent lost in printing

explanation.definitionFit: A French phrase meaning backwards, and the title of a collection of stories by Marcel Aymé.

clue.text: Possible nominal disadvantage for Mrs Humphry Ward

definitions.text: Possible nominal disadvantage for Mrs Humphry Ward

parts.words: Possible nominal disadvantage for Mrs Humphry Ward
parts.note: the novelist's surname turned round becomes a verb, and an instruction to put her name back gives a word for a handicap

explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Humphry Ward was a Victorian novelist; her name WARD read back to front gives DRAW, and 'Ward back' is a punning description of a downside.
explanation.definitionFit: A disadvantage or snag, which a reversed name might literally be.

clue.text: Sixteenth-century ballad found in untidy sideboard

indicators.note: an untidy piece of furniture has its contents jumbled, so the letters of sideboard are rearranged

explanation.surface: An old printed ballad turns up in a messy sideboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'untidy' rearranges the letters of SIDEBOARD. A broadside was a ballad printed on one side of a single sheet.
explanation.definitionFit: A song printed on one side of a large sheet and sold in the streets, popular from Tudor times.

clue.text: He got the bird in Barnes book

definitions.text: He got the bird in Barnes book

parts.words: He got the bird in Barnes book
parts.note: Julian Barnes's novel is named after a stuffed parrot owned by a French novelist

explanation.walkthrough: 'got the bird' usually means being booed; here it means owning the parrot of Julian Barnes's novel Flaubert's Parrot.
explanation.definitionFit: The French novelist whose stuffed parrot gives Julian Barnes's 1984 novel its title.

clue.text: A coney-catching rascal with a bulbous red nose

definitions.text: A coney-catching rascal with a bulbous red nose

parts.words: A coney-catching rascal with a bulbous red nose
parts.note: Falstaff's drunken follower in Shakespeare, mocked for his fiery face; coney-catching is Elizabethan for swindling

explanation.walkthrough: 'coney-catching' is Elizabethan slang for cheating; the red-nosed rogue is one of Falstaff's companions in the Henry plays and The Merry Wives of Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: Falstaff's red-nosed crony, called a 'coney-catching rascal' in The Merry Wives of Windsor.

clue.text: Bones of Greek mountain

definitions.meaning: the Latin plural for skeletal bones
a peak in Thessaly that giants piled on Pelion in myth

explanation.definitionFit: Latin for bones, and the mountain in Thessaly famous from the myth of piling Pelion on it.

clue.text: French-born US composer from Italian city

definitions.meaning: Edgard, the Paris-born modernist who made his career in New York, pioneer of electronic music
a city in Lombardy north-west of Milan

explanation.definitionFit: Surname of the modernist composer Edgard Varèse, and a Lombard city north-west of Milan.

clue.text: A brief moment to scowl badly about gilding

indicators.note: the rearranged frown is placed around the short moment
done badly, the letters of the frowning word are rearranged

parts.note: to lour is to scowl or frown
mo is short for moment, as in 'half a mo'

explanation.surface: Someone wastes a moment frowning crossly at some gold decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' is a link word here; 'brief moment' is the colloquial 'just a mo', and the scowl word is the old verb meaning to frown or look sullen, as a sky can.
explanation.definitionFit: Gilded bronze or gold-coloured alloy used to decorate furniture, a form of gilding.

clue.text: Making pigment is a terrible chore

indicators.note: a terrible version of the word chore has its letters messed up

explanation.surface: Grinding colours for paint is an awful job.
explanation.definitionFit: An earthy yellow or brown iron-oxide colouring used in paints.

clue.text: Loyal schoolfriend of David's treasurer goes to the bad

definitions.text: Loyal schoolfriend of David's treasurer goes to the bad

parts.words: Loyal schoolfriend of David's treasurer goes to the bad
parts.note: Tommy, David Copperfield's faithful friend from Salem House school, who stands by him through Micawber's exposure of the fraudster Heep

explanation.walkthrough: The Dickens character is David Copperfield's steadfast schoolfriend Tommy; the second half points to the plot in which money goes astray.
explanation.definitionFit: Surname of Tommy, David Copperfield's loyal friend from schooldays in Dickens's novel.

clue.text: The opponent of Desmond Bagley

parts.note: a thriller title by Desmond Bagley, whose name means a foe

explanation.walkthrough: Desmond Bagley was a British thriller writer; one of his novels has a title meaning foe, so the clue reads both as the book and as an adversary.
explanation.definitionFit: A word for a foe or adversary, and the title of a 1977 thriller by Desmond Bagley.

clue.text: Updike subject in adobe church

indicators.note: the name sits inside the words adobe church, straddling them

explanation.surface: John Updike writes about a mud-brick place of worship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals letters inside 'adoBE CHurch'. Henry Bech is the Jewish novelist hero of several Updike books.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Bech, the fictional writer who is the hero of Updike's Bech books.

clue.text: Deep mines I reconstruct, discovering sleepy philosopher

indicators.note: to reconstruct the words Deep mines I is to rebuild their letters in a new order

explanation.surface: A miner rebuilding deep shafts stumbles on a drowsy thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reconstruct' rearranges DEEP MINES I. The Cretan philosopher Epimenides was said to have slept in a cave for fifty-seven years.
explanation.definitionFit: Cretan seer famed for a legendary sleep of fifty-seven years in a cave.

clue.text: "-at his utmost need / By those his former bounty fed" (Dryden)

definitions.text: "-at his utmost need / By those his former bounty fed" (Dryden)

parts.words: "-at his utmost need / By those his former bounty fed" (Dryden)
parts.note: the missing word from Dryden's Alexander's Feast, about Darius abandoned by those he had once fed

explanation.walkthrough: The lines come from Dryden's Alexander's Feast, describing the fallen Persian king Darius, abandoned by those he once supported.
explanation.definitionFit: Abandoned, the word completing Dryden's line about the fallen Darius.

clue.text: Waugh the diarist?

explanation.definitionFit: Forename of the novelist Waugh, and surname of John Evelyn, the seventeenth-century diary writer.
